summary: Sets out how values for the Point-to-Point Protocol, such as protocol numbers, are assigned by IANA, and what review each kind of assignment needs. The goal is to keep PPP extensions orderly while discouraging frivolous additions.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a new rule can be added to a big game, this document explains who must say yes and how it gets written in the official rulebook.

questions: how are ppp protocol numbers assigned
what requires ietf consensus in ppp
subtitle: Rules for registering new protocol numbers and values in the Point-to-Point Protocol

tldr.problem: PPP had many proposed extensions of questionable value, and the IANA was assigning protocol numbers on a first-come, first-served basis without review, making it difficult to maintain quality control.
tldr.mechanism: This Best Current Practice changes the policy for assigning values in 13 PPP namespaces (protocol numbers, configuration options, authentication algorithms, and others) from first-come, first-served to require IETF Consensus, usually through the PPP Extensions working group.
tldr.outcome: The policy ensures that new PPP extensions are subject to review and prevents frivolous additions to the protocol.

today: RFC 3818 is in effect and establishes the standard policy for PPP value assignments. It reflects the working group's commitment to maintaining PPP quality while allowing measured evolution of the protocol.

sections.title: The Problem with Unreviewed Extensions
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) is a mature protocol with many subprotocols and extensions. Each extension typically needs assigned values from several PPP namespaces, such as protocol numbers, configuration option types, and algorithm identifiers.

Historically, IANA used a first-come, first-served policy for these assignments, meaning anyone could request a number without review. This led to proposals for extensions of questionable value being assigned numbers without oversight, conflicting with the PPP Extensions working group's goal of defending against enhancements that add little benefit.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP is an old protocol with many add-ons. People were asking for new numbers without anyone checking if the add-on was actually useful.

sections.title: New Assignment Requirements
sections.content:
This RFC changes the assignment policy for 13 PPP namespaces to require IETF Consensus, typically obtained through the Point-to-Point Protocol Extensions (pppext) working group. These namespaces include protocol numbers, LCP and IPCP codes, configuration option types for various PPP features, authentication algorithms, and others.

Requesters must now justify their proposals, and they are subject to review by the working group and the broader IETF community before receiving an assigned value.
sections.plainLanguage: For 13 different types of numbers that PPP uses, someone must now convince the committee the idea is worth adding to the rulebook.

sections.title: Scope and Implementation
sections.content:
The new IETF Consensus requirement applies to assignments in the following address spaces: PPP DLL Protocol Numbers, LCP and IPCP Codes, LCP Configuration Option Types, CCP Configuration Option Types, CHAP Authentication Algorithms, LCP FCS-Alternatives, Multilink Endpoint Discriminator Classes, LCP Callback Operation Fields, and others.

This policy ensures that PPP extensions are carefully evaluated, discouraging frivolous additions while still allowing the protocol to evolve in useful ways.
sections.plainLanguage: The committee now reviews requests for protocol numbers, code options, and other configuration items before granting them.
